Although for obvious reasons I do not feel myself at liberty to enter into details with regard to the fortifications, it may be stated that all that two of the most accomplished engineer officers of the Confederacy?General Lee and Beauregard?could suggest or devise has been done to strengthen the town on its land side. General Lee, before he was moved to Virginia and assigned his present high position, was for some time in command of Charleston, and by him the first line of land defenses was planned and executed. The line ran from Fort Johnson to Fort Moultrie, embracing at the junction of Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie, forming a perfect work of earthworks and embrasures, extending from the north to the Ashley River on the south.

But unfortunately this beautiful morning has found our country disarrayed; the Union, if not al- ready dissolved, is on the verge of disso- lution, and every thing pertaining to Na- tional affairs in the worst confusion. When I wrote you last by Pony, I told you of the resignation of Messrs. Cobb and Cass, of the Cabinet; since then Secretary Floyd has resigned. "Old Buck seems to change with every wind, and will soon have no cabinet left. Cobb left him because Old Buck had de- termined to enforce the laws in South Carolina; Cass, because he would not enforce them, and now Floyd leaves be- cause Old Buck is disposed to enforce them. It is not known certainly yet who will be appointed in Floyd's place. Since I wrote you, South Carolina has declared herself independent, and seems determined to go it on her own hook. The "Mobile Register" was produced this morning by a report, which obtained currency and credit in important circles, that Major Anderson would be withdrawn from Fort Sumter. As no official action has been taken by the Administration, no answer is indicated to weigh with the public, though it has made some impression here. It is well known that Major Anderson cannot now be reinforced without imminent danger of a serious collision. Two steamers of light draft, with supplies of men and provisions, have been in readiness for some time to make the attempt whenever ordered, under the command of an officer who is willing to take the risk, and feels confident of success. But the military preparations in and outside of the Harbor of Charleston render any such experiment hazardous, unless sustained by a heavy naval force, which could be used now, as the main ship channel is entirely clear of obstructions. The War Department has obtained a detailed statement of the stock of provisions in Fort Sumter, and it is abundant for a considerable time, except in fresh beef, which is not sufficient for over thirty days. One of the first and most important questions, therefore, to press the Administration will be, whether Major Anderson will be supplied or withdrawn. That decision cannot be made until an-

Its weakest point is on the south side, of which the masonry is not only weaker than the other sides, but it is not protected by any flank fire which would sweep the landing wharf. Once landed, a party could have easily effected an entrance. The work was designed for an armament of one hundred and forty guns of various calibers. Two tiers of guns are in casemates, while the upper one is open, or in barbette, the lower tier for forty-two-pounder Paixhan guns, second tier eight and ten-inch columbiads, and the barbette tier for mortars and twenty four-pounder guns. We learn from Thomas Kearns, one of the garrison of Fort Sumter, many interesting particulars in relation to that work. Our informant left there only a few weeks ago and is now in this city. He states that in Fort Sumter there are one hundred and four guns ready for action, about fifty-two (one and a half) of which are ten-inch columbiads, the remainder being eight and nine-inch Dahlgrens and howitzers. There are four heavy mortars in the fort, one being stationed at its corner. There are about twelve rifled guns in the works, but in consequence of the explosion of one of those guns, by which an officer of high rank narrowly escaped losing his life, it had been determined not to place any more reliance upon such pieces.

I am General, Very respectfully, your obedient servant. U. S. GRANT, Brigadier Gen. Grant immediately after the Headquarters District West Tennessee, Fort Donelson, Feb. 17, 1862. The general commanding takes great pleasure in congratulating the troops of this command for the triumph over rebellion, gained by their the 13th, 14th, and 16th instant. For four successive nights, without shelter during the most inclement weather known in this latitude, they faced the enemy in large force in a position chosen by himself. Though strongly fortified by nature, all the additional safety added. With borne, prepared at all attack, and with continuous guards suggested by science without a murmur this times to receive skirmishing all day, resulting ultimately in surrender without conditions. The victory achieved is not only great in the effect it will have in breaking down rebellion, but has elicited the greatest number of prisoners. Fort Donelson will hereafter be marked in capitals on the map of the united country, and the men who fought the battle will live in the memory of a grateful people. By order, O. S. Grant, Brigadier General Commanding GEN. McCLERNAND'S ORDER OF THE DAY. Headquarters First Div Fort Donelson, Feb. 15, 1862.

The crossing of the Potomac by Lee's army was a great surprise to the Federal Commander, Meade, who expected to have caught him on the northern bank near Williamsport and fought the decisive battle of the War. But Lee successfully achieved the passage of his main army, with 7,000 train wagons, losing only a brigade of his rear guard, some 1,500 men captured. Lee's movements are not clearly defined, but he is supposed to be going up the Shenandoah Valley, with a view of covering Richmond, and resuming operations on the old theatres of war in Virginia. Meade has also crossed the Potomac, lower down the river, and has the advantage of a shorter march than Lee, to gain any point in Eastern Virginia either may desire to possess. The ultra eastern press are already muttering dissatisfaction at Meade for having allowed Lee to escape annihilation; rumors are abroad that he is to be superseded by Grant, but this is not probable. The anti-conscription riots in the North and the reported discontent with the Confederate government in North Carolina, though not regular military operations, are nevertheless marked features of the War.

Mr. Calhoun, pastor of the Presbyterian profession, who was requested to open the meeting with prayer, which he did accordingly, in a most appropriate and patriotic manner. Mr. Wise, from the committee appointed Aug. 23, reported the following resolution for the adoption of the Convention: Whereas, it is the deliberate and con- scientious opinion of this Convention, that an attempt at the coercion of a Sovereign State is in direct contravention of the letter and spirit of the United States Constitution, and that, while it is the desire of Virginia to expend that in due course of law, her rights as a sovereign, she is unwilling to precipitate the dreadful and calamitous issues of civil war, in which the effusion of blood and the devastation of the country must ensue, and which can be averted by the concurrent action of all the States.

Davenport Democrat. The venerable and learned Judge Witherell, of the Circuit court at Detroit, Michigan, has vindicated the majesty of the civil law in a most refreshing manner. Some little time ago a soldier fired upon and killed a hackman of that city, by order of the wounded officers. These perpetrators of murder were arrested and held by the local civil authorities; whereupon the war department at Washington demanded that they should be handed over to the federal military authorities. It is in interposing a flat refusal to this demand that Judge Witherell has maintained the supremacy of the civil law.

The account of capture of Fort Pillow says that on the morning of 12th, Forrest, Chalmers, and McCullough, with from 6,000 to 8,000 men, attacked the Fort garrisoned by 300 of 13th Tennessee cavalry and 200 negroes. Some citizens were inside the Fort who fought well. Women and children went over on an island. The enemy were hidden and fired from under cover for some time. Surrender was demanded several times without effect. At last, the enemy formed into two columns and made a direct assault. Troops in the fort fought like heroes until rebels were seen on breastworks, when negro troops gave way and ran down under the river bank. White troops were directed to take their places, but derangement in lines could not be remedied, and the enemy poured in force. Gunboats, seven in number, threw 240 shells, but did no damage to the enemy. Our troops spiked three guns, who afterward set fire to everything combustible, burning all houses in town. Negroes who had taken refuge under the river bank were shot wherever found, notwithstanding surrender. Fifty white troops were also shot and wounded after surrender. Accounts in regard to the policy of the administration respecting Forts Sumter and Pickens are becoming more contradictory daily. Texas advices state that Col. The Secretary shows an aggregate of appropriations already made of seventy-nine million seven hundred and ten thousand and eighteen dollars and seventy-eight cents, and then proceeds to state that the additional estimates for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1861, including the deficiency caused by the application of $6,298,837 to the service of the preceding year will require additional appropriations for the civil list, foreign intercourse, and miscellaneous objects, $831,160; for the Interior Department, $431,523; for the War Department, $185,296,379.19; for the Navy Department, $30,009,520; in the aggregate, $217,168,050.50. In addition to the demands upon the Treasury, it will be necessary to provide for the redemption of Treasury notes due and maturing to the amount of $12,039,861, and for the payment of the interest on the public debt to be created during the year, which, computed for an average of six months, may be estimated at nine million. The whole amount required for the fiscal year 1862 may therefore be stated at $318,519,581.87. Provision is made for the interest on the existing public debt in the sum of nearly $66,000,000 already appropriated for the year 1862.

THE CONFEDERATE. WEEKLY. AUGUST 14, 1864. Pffte. It is a very easy matter to draw the line on which fair and legitimate propositions may be made, on which rightful opinions may be held, and on which full discussion may be had. It was not always wise, but it was never criminal to express a wish for peace, to urge the government to make every effort to commence negotiations for peace. This was not always wise, because, up to a very late period the enemy had shown no inclination whatever to listen to any terms, except the humiliation of an abject submission. Neither the Federal Government nor the Yankee people had given promise of any inclination for other terms. Until a late period the fortunes of the war varied; and though the true brave, patriot spirit looked assuredly for a final success, it was obliged to nerve itself for the endurance of much trial and danger, in order to its achievement. Last summer and fall, when the peace cry in North Carolina was most noisy, was a most inopportune and inappropriate period for such demonstration. Then, the balance of success was with the north. Disaster had settled heavily upon us, and the cry for peace in such a time, was like the cry of "enough" by the beaten pugilist when he gives up the fight.
